PAPER: JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH Yao et al Original Paper Factors Influencing Continuance Intention for Online Consultations Among Survivors of Cancer: Grounded Theory Study Yutang Yao1*, MD; Musi Zhang2*, BSN; Shanshan Peng2, BMed; Zhuzhong Cheng1, MD; Yun Duan1, BMed 1Department of Nuclear Medicine, Sichuan Cancer Hospital & Institute, Sichuan Cancer Center, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, Sichuan, China 2Department of Radiation Oncology, Sichuan Cancer Hospital & Institute, Sichuan Cancer Center, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, Sichuan, China *these authors contributed equally Corresponding Author: Yun Duan, BMed Department of Nuclear Medicine Sichuan Cancer Hospital & Institute, Sichuan Cancer Center University of Electronic Science and Technology of China 55 Renmin South Rd Section 4 Chengdu, Sichuan, 610041 China Phone: 86 02885420214 Email: duanyun163@126.com Abstract Background: Online consultation platforms have become an important component of survivorship care for patients with cancer, offering flexible access to oncology expertise between scheduled visits. However, evidence on what drives the willingness of survivors of cancer to continue using online consultations after initial adoption remains limited in China. A better understanding of continuance intention is needed to inform survivor-centered digital health strategies. Objective: This study aimed to explore the influencing factors of continued use of online consultations among survivors of cancer in southwest China and develop a grounded theoretical model explaining continuance intention. Methods: A grounded theory qualitative design was used. A total of 26 adult survivors of cancer with diverse demographic and clinical characteristics were purposively recruited from a tertiary cancer center in southwest China. All participants had used online consultations at least once in the preceding year. Semistructured telephone interviews were audio recorded; transcribed verbatim; and analyzed using open, axial, and selective coding with constant comparison until theoretical saturation was reached. During selective coding, categories and their relationships were integrated and iteratively refined to construct a grounded theoretical model of continuance intention. Results: Six interrelated domains influenced survivors’ continued use of online consultation platforms: platform quality, physician competence, user perception, individual condition, external context, and privacy concerns. Platform quality and physician competence influenced user perception of usefulness, reassurance, and trust, which functioned as a mediator of continued use. Individual condition, including health status, health literacy, and psychological needs, influenced both perceived usefulness and reliance on online consultations. External context, especially family encouragement, peer recommendations, and availability of local oncology services, directly facilitated or constrained continued use. Privacy concerns moderated how survivors balanced perceived benefits against risks of data misuse, stigma, and unwanted disclosure of cancer history. Survivors described online consultations as offering rapid guidance and emotional support that complemented hospital-based care but reported discontinuation when interactions were delayed or impersonal or when perceived privacy risks outweighed the benefits. Conclusions: The willingness of survivors of cancer to continue using online consultation platforms depends on multiple interrelated factors beyond traditional technological usability. Sustained engagement is shaped by survivors’ perceptions of usefulness and trust, physician empathy and timeliness, family encouragement, and acceptance of privacy trade-offs. The theoretical model advances understanding of digital health continuance in oncology and offers practical guidance for developing survivor-centered online consultation services. JSON: Name: oncology_online_consultation_continuance_model Title: Sequential mixed-methods validation and quantitative testing of a grounded-theory model of continuance intention for online oncology consultations Short Hypothesis: Perceived usefulness and trust mediate the positive effects of platform quality and physician competence on survivors' continuance intention for online consultations, with privacy concerns moderating the mediated pathways such that higher privacy concerns weaken the indirect effects. Related Work: Prior work on digital health continuance has primarily relied on technology-focused models (e.g., TAM, ECM) that emphasize perceived usefulness, ease of use, satisfaction, habit, and trust; empirical studies across chronic disease and general mHealth contexts have shown these factors predict ongoing use but often omit clinical relational and contextual variables. Oncology and survivorship studies have documented benefits of telemedicine for symptom management and psychosocial support and highlighted the importance of clinician responsiveness, but most oncology work is descriptive, focused on adoption or short-term satisfaction, or limited to single cancer types or populations. Existing studies rarely integrate family/caregiver influence, survivors' health status and psychological needs, institutional affiliation, and privacy risk negotiation into a single framework. Limitations in current approaches include reliance on cross-sectional convenience samples, lack of theory-grounded mixed-method validation, insufficient modeling of mediation/moderation relationships, and limited attention to sociocultural contexts (e.g., family facilitation, hospital-affiliation trust) that may drive continuance among cancer survivors. Abstract: Problem: Survivors of cancer may adopt online consultation platforms but discontinue use, limiting long-term survivorship benefits; existing models emphasize technology factors but underrepresent relational, clinical, and privacy dynamics. Approach: We propose a sequential mixed-methods research pipeline to validate and quantitatively test a grounded-theory model of continuance intention that integrates platform quality, physician competence, user perception (usefulness and trust), individual condition, external context (family/peer support, local service availability), and privacy concerns. Methods: Conduct a multicenter cross-sectional survey (N≈600) with validated multi-item scales and a longitudinal subsample (n≈200) for three-month behavior follow-up; analyze using exploratory and confirmatory structural equation modeling with mediation and moderated mediation tests and multiple-group analyses (urban vs rural). Contribution: The study will provide a tested causal model quantifying direct, indirect, and moderating effects driving continuance intention in oncology survivorship, enabling precise targeting of interventions. Expected outcome: Empirically supported parameter estimates and model fit metrics that identify the relative contributions of technological, relational, and privacy factors to sustained use of online oncology consultations. Experiments: Datasets: Multicenter survey dataset collected from adult cancer survivors (N=600) recruited from at least 4 tertiary cancer centers across urban and semiurban/rural regions in China; inclusion: age ≥18, confirmed cancer diagnosis, at least one online consultation in past 12 months; longitudinal substudy: n=200 recontacted at 3 months to record actual repeat use. Measures: Multi-item validated or adapted scales (7-point Likert) for platform quality (service reliability, info quality), physician competence (expertise, communication, timeliness), user perception (perceived usefulness, reassurance, trust), individual condition (health status index, health literacy scale, psychological need score), external context (family support index, peer recommendation frequency, local oncology access score), privacy concerns (sensitivity and disclosure risk), outcome: continuance intention scale and observed repeat-use binary outcome at 3 months. Baselines: (A) TAM/ECM baseline model (perceived usefulness and satisfaction only), (B) model without external context and individual condition, (C) model without privacy moderator. Evaluation metrics: SEM fit indices (CFI≥0.95, TLI≥0.95, RMSEA≤0.06, SRMR≤0.08), standardized path coefficients, R-squared for continuance intention, indirect effects significance via bootstrap (5,000 samples) confidence intervals, moderation tested with interaction terms and conditional indirect effects, classification metrics (AUC, sensitivity, specificity) for longitudinal repeat-use prediction. Experimental setup: Randomly split N=600 into exploratory (n=200) for EFA and measurement refinement, and confirmatory sample (n=400) for CFA and SEM; perform measurement invariance tests across urban vs rural and age groups; ablation study: compare variance explained and fit when removing each of the six domains sequentially; sensitivity analyses: control for digital literacy and prior telehealth frequency; pre-register analysis plan and power calculations targeting detection of small-to-moderate indirect effects (standardized indirect effect d=0.15) with power 0.8, requiring approx. N=400-600 for SEM. Risk Factors and Limitations: Self-report measurement bias and social desirability affecting scales for trust, privacy concerns, and intention; cross-sectional SEM limits causal inferences despite mediation modeling; sample recruitment bias toward hospital-connected survivors and those willing to complete phone/online surveys, reducing representativeness; measurement validity risk if adapted scales lack psychometric validation in Chinese oncology survivorship populations; digital literacy and age confounding may produce spurious associations; multicollinearity among constructs (e.g., trust and perceived usefulness) may inflate standard errors and obscure distinct effects; missing data and attrition in longitudinal subsample may reduce power and bias longitudinal outcome estimates; limited geographic generalizability outside studied regions and health systems; potential small effect sizes requiring larger samples than planned; inability to observe unmeasured institutional or platform-specific policies that influence continuance (e.g., pricing changes) which may limit external validity.
